**Hydrogeological Dynamics, Behavioural Clustering and Management Intervention Analysis at Newborough Warren Coastal Sand Dune Aquifer, Wales**

*A state-space modelling and empirical analysis of groundwater behaviour, forest management, dune scraping, hydrological boundaries and critical rainfall forecasting*

M. Hollingham \| June 2026

ORCID: 0000-0003-0253-9301

Contact : [**martin.hollingham+nrg@gmail.com**](mailto:martin.hollingham+nrg@gmail.com)

**Abstract**

Coastal sand dune aquifers are ecologically sensitive systems whose groundwater regimes determine the persistence of legally protected dune slack habitats. Newborough Warren, a 1,300-hectare Special Area of Conservation (SAC) on the Isle of Anglesey, Wales, has undergone sustained water table decline over recent decades, threatening the humid dune slack communities for which the site is designated. This study presents a low-cost, reproducible, data-driven analytical pipeline of 50 steps across 17 phases, requiring only monthly dipwell readings and publicly available climate data from the nearest meteorological station. The pipeline is applied to a network of 88 wells monitored over 2005--2026, integrating hierarchical clustering, Pearson affinity analysis, a three-term state-space model (SSM) parametrizing recharge, atmospheric draw and head-dependent drainage, comparative model benchmarking, water table fluctuation specific yield estimation, dune scraping and clearfell BACI analysis with three-counterfactual ANCOVA climate correction, cluster-level water balance decomposition, per-well spatial coefficient mapping, critical rainfall threshold (P_flood) forecasting, seasonal prediction equations, and a per-well scenario framework for climate and forest management projections. The approach is designed for replication at comparable coastal dune sites using minimal equipment and no specialist modelling infrastructure.

Hierarchical clustering (Ward\'s linkage, k = 5, selected for behavioural resolution and mechanistic interpretability, with four of five clusters confirmed by bootstrap stability analysis) identifies five hydrogeological units spanning a behavioural spectrum from shallow pan to deep sponge to canopy sponge. The eastern open dune (C1 Lake Edge, C2 Dune) responds rapidly to rainfall with high recharge sensitivity, with drainage fastest at the lake-coupled C1 (Lumped Catchment Storage Coefficient, LCSC = 21.8%) and slower at the larger, more representative C2 Dune archetype (LCSC = 25.2%). The Western Residual (C3) acts as a deep buffer (LCSC = 28.0%). Two Forest clusters (C4 Main Forest, C5 Coastal Forest) share elevated LCSC values (40.4%, 41.2%) reflecting canopy interception of approximately 24% of rainfall (Freeman, 2008), but differ in setting: C4 sits on the elevated ridge flank (atmospheric draw coefficient β₂ = 2.56) while C5 occupies the lower coastal ground (β₂ = 1.27). Per-well analysis within the forest zone shows that elevation alone explains 96% of β₂ variance, indicating topographic position --- and the substrate inferred to underlie it --- as the major control on the atmospheric draw coefficient, with depth-coupling and other factors also acting. The co-temporal amplification field (Figure 65) shows C4 Main Forest to be the most climate-volatile zone on the site, with a mean spring swing 1.72 times the network mean between canonical dry and wet years. This over-response reflects two positional factors: thin saturated thickness over irregular bedrock, and the forest\'s occupation of the hydraulic high of the aquifer, furthest from any lateral discharge boundary and therefore without the damping that lake-edge or coastal proximity provides. Of the two forested clusters only C5\'s β₂ falls below the open-dune range; C4\'s β₂ is genuinely elevated, an identifiability diagnostic having found the drainage coefficient cleanly resolved and no β₂--β₃ degeneracy, and reflects position and substrate rather than canopy. Whether the canopy suppresses summer atmospheric draw is unresolved on the present evidence, and the stronger canopy evidence remains the recharge suppression captured in the lower β₁ of both forest clusters. Once corrected for interception, C4\'s WTF-derived specific yield falls within the open-dune range and the interpolated yield surface shows no discontinuity at the cluster margins; the C5 estimate is consistent with this but is the least reliable in the network and is treated as weakly corroborative. On this evidence the plantation\'s distinctive β-coefficient signature derives largely from canopy boundary conditions at the surface rather than from differences in subsurface storage architecture.

The SSM outperforms the traditional linear model in iterative forecasting (median per-well NSE improvement +0.82; 65 of 66 wells with positive NSE vs 30 of 66 for TLM), demonstrating that explicit parametrization of head-dependent drainage memory is essential for long-range prediction in this aquifer. The framework requires only monthly rainfall and temperature from a single climate station and is operationally transferable to other coastal dune aquifers and, in principle, to other groundwater-fed wetland settings. The water balance closes to within 2.5% at all five clusters under a displacement formulation. Seasonal prediction equations establish that antecedent summer minimum depth, not winter rainfall, is the dominant predictor of winter flooding potential. The ecological significance is acute: the entire gradient from SD15b wet slack through SD16 dry slack to the SD16 recovery threshold spans only 37 cm of summer minimum depth (Curreli et al., 2013), so all management interventions must be evaluated on their summer minimum effect.

Dune scraping at CEH36 produced a paired summer minimum shift of +195 mm (p = 0.004) --- more than half the SD15b--SD16 ecological gradient --- identified by three independent methods (raw BACI +129 mm, synthetic control +137 mm, SSM forward residual +73 mm). The benefit persisted through the post-felling period while the paired control deteriorated, and the operational zone for this intervention is the C1/C2 area where P_flood thresholds remain achievable. CEH18 and CEH21, scraped in October 2023, showed limited responses that did not survive correction for background drift --- consistent with progressive coastal boundary retreat overwhelming the intervention at the more coastal sites. A reproducible off-site drawdown is measured at the nearest long-record uphill well (−55 mm and −54 mm at the 2015 and 2023 scrapes), consistent with the relief-drainage mechanism by which a scraped low collects lateral inflow and draws down its neighbours; the wider neighbour-drawdown magnitude at greater distances remains a modelled scenario the 31-month record cannot resolve, and no distance-decay is detectable in the drainage coefficient. Because scraping operates through the same physical mechanism as coastal erosion --- lowering ground elevation to increase the drainage gradient --- its spatial placement determines whether it complements or exacerbates the existing coastal drainage regime.

A five-tier, 17-well BACI experiment with three counterfactual controls tested the December 2017 clearfell of 8.4 ha of Corsican pine. Against the Forest control --- the most direct test, comparing felled wells against unfelled forest sharing the same canopy and substrate --- the ANCOVA-BACI detected a significant clearfell step of +113 mm at the single in-compartment Impact well WMC3 (p = 0.002); the Edge-tier step of +29 mm was not statistically significant (p = 0.25), and synthetic extension of within-compartment FE wells returned a clearfell step of +80 mm (p \< 0.001). The clearfell signal is concentrated in the mean monthly water level rather than in summer minima at the felled wells, where felled and unfelled wells tracked each other. The coefficient decomposition reveals a site-wide decline in recharge sensitivity (β₁) across all five tiers of the BACI network, independent of management intervention and consistent with changing within-month rainfall distribution. This β₁ decline is the strongest candidate mechanism for the observed summer minimum deterioration and operates independently of canopy cover, affecting felled and unfelled wells equally.

The scenario framework evaluates clearfell, 50% thinning and broadleaf conversion alongside UKCP18 climate projections. Clearfell and thinning produce small positive net annual responses at the forest clusters (clearfell: C4 +8.6 mm w.e./month, C5 +10.9 mm; thinning: +4.3 and +5.4 mm respectively). Broadleaf conversion produces a small net annual effect (C4 −0.7 mm; C5 +1.7 mm): the interception reduction from 24% to 15% during the recharge season is offset by the growing-season transpiration penalty. Forest management perturbations do not propagate measurably to the open dune clusters where ecological need is greatest. The forestry-scenario magnitudes are substantially smaller than the climate-driven changes (C4 dry-scenario −12.2 mm; wet-scenario +6.0 mm), indicating that climate trajectory dominates over canopy management at this site.

Network-wide summer minimum depths have declined at all five clusters, with C1 and C5 statistically significant, C2 marginal, and C3 and C4 non-significant. C5 Coastal Forest shows the steepest decline in both seasons and is the only cluster with a significant winter decline. A network-scale gradient regression of per-well summer-minimum slopes against perpendicular distance to the eroding western shoreline attributes the whole of C5\'s exceptional decline to a coastal-retreat signal, and slightly more (n = 3 in the gradient subset; see Section 4.8.2). The fitted coast-edge anomaly is −26 mm yr⁻¹ at 150 m from the shoreline over an inland reach of 895 m, and C5 sits closest to the shore of any cluster, so the gradient accounts for 113 % of its observed decline on the balanced basis --- a share above 100 % being possible because each component is a rate rather than a share of a fitted total. The two other candidate mechanisms, amplified head response under thin saturated thickness at the coastal margin and progressive canopy maturation, are therefore not required to close C5\'s decline, though neither is excluded by it. C1 and C2 lie beyond the fitted inland reach; C4\'s mean distance falls marginally inside it and carries a component too small to resolve.

The deterioration is concentrated in the summer season, consistent with the observed warming trend (post-2013 period +0.94°C above baseline) and increasing atmospheric evaporative demand. Monthly decomposition of the RAF Valley PET record shows significant increases in May (+0.066 mm month⁻¹ yr⁻¹, p = 0.002), June (+0.047, p = 0.030) and July (+0.062, p = 0.006), providing a physical mechanism for the observed secular deepening concentrated in the early-summer period when the water table is falling from its spring peak. A bootstrap of the C1 summer-minimum linear trend places the median crossing year of the SD16 dry-slack viability threshold at 2028 (90% CI 2022--2049), and the cluster is no longer approaching SD16 but oscillating across it --- four of the eight most recent observed summer minima have already exceeded the SD16 depth.

The two ecologically referenced metrics diverge sharply in their climate exposure: the five-year mean spring water level (MSL5; van Willegen et al. 2025), which describes the sustained baseline within which dune-slack vegetation establishes, is projected to shift by only 21--39 mm under the 2080s trajectory, three to five times less than the parallel summer-minimum deepening, so that the spring baseline remains within its present Curreli regime at every cluster while the summer minimum --- the binding ecological constraint --- deteriorates across the network. On the MSL5 baseline the open-dune clusters (C1, C2) sit comfortably within the wet-slack regime throughout the record, whereas the Coastal Forest cluster (C5) sits below the dry-slack threshold throughout; the scraping benefit is expressed on this baseline metric as well as on summer minima, while the clearfell recovery is not. An empirical comparison of five-year mean spring water levels (MSL5) between the pre-clearfell baseline (window end 2017, springs 2013--2017) and the current period (window end 2023, springs 2019--2023) shows a site-wide secular deepening of 97 mm with the largest declines at the south-western coastal margin (CEH22 −229 mm, C5 coastal members −150 to −153 mm); no spatially distinct signal attributable to either the 2015 scraping or the 2017 clearfell is detectable above the ±25 mm measurement noise threshold. This is consistent with the BACI finding that the clearfell recovery is expressed in the monthly-mean water level rather than in five-year spring means.

Independently, MSL5 as implemented is cross-validated against the co-located Ellenberg-F vegetation moisture of van Willegen et al. (2025), reproducing their published spring levels to within \~11 mm and predicting mean Ellenberg-F between wells (r = 0.83, n = 18). An equilibrium wetness index derived from the state-space coefficients alone (independent of MSL5) is statistically indistinguishable from MSL5 as an Ellenberg-F predictor (Williams p = 0.81), and, calibrated onto the MSL5 scale, reconstructs observed spring levels across the open dune to 61 mm RMSE, generalizing to wells outside the vegetation-calibrated set --- showing that dynamics-only coefficients encode ecohydrological state. It is scoped to the open dune (degrading in the forest) and its practical edge is a shorter required record, not simpler construction.

The P_flood threshold equations, seasonal prediction equations and scenario framework, together with live Equilibrium Wetness Index (EWI) and five-year mean spring level (MSL5) monitoring, are implemented as interactive tools hosted on the Newborough Warren Groundwater Research project page. The monitoring evidence characterizes canopy removal as a winter-recharge intervention: it produces a detectable mean water table recovery at the Forest clusters, but its effect on summer minimum depth --- the metric that determines dune slack viability --- is set by the same site-wide β₁ decline that affects unfelled forest and open dune wells alike. The operational domain for direct hydrological intervention lies in targeted scraping in the C1/C2 zone where P_flood thresholds remain achievable, against a climate trajectory that is the binding constraint on all outcomes. The intervention window is measured in one to two decades.
